qAndA.answer: A Galilean telescope produces a non-inverted image, making it more convenient for terrestrial observation. Additionally, it is physically shorter than a Keplerian telescope.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Building a Keplerian Telescope requires two converging lenses, an objective and an
eyepiece, aligned coaxially and sharing a focal point.
Parallel ways enter the objective, converge at the shared focal point, invert and are
made parallel again by the eyepiece.
The magnification and increased intensity are represented by the tighter spacing of the
rays as they enter the eye.
We find the focal point of the eyepiece by focusing the image of the hallway on a sheet
of paper.
While objects infinitely far away would focus to a point, objects that are only much further
away than the focal length focus to an image that is barely past the focal point.
We then focus the objective lens the same way on the same sheet of paper.
Once both lenses share a focal point, they form a working telescope.
As you can see, they form a focused, inverted image of the hallway.
A Galilean telescope uses a similar converging objective lens, but a diverging eyepiece.
Again, these two lenses share a focus, but now the eyepiece is inside the objective's
length.
Starting with the existing capillary in telescope, the converging eyepiece is replaced with a diverging
lens.
The objective is then brought closer until the telescope comes into focus.
This Galilean telescope is not only much shorter in length than the capillary, it also
produces a non-inverted image.

youtube_description:
This video was made for the Refraction and Thin Lenses Lab for PHYS 102 and PHYS 151. 
A Keplerian and Galilean telescope are constructed on a table top using simple lenses. 

The video begins a ray optics explanation of A Keplerian telescope. A pair of converging lenses are then focused on a shared point to create a working telescope. After a ray optics description of a Galilean telescope, the converging eyepiece of the telescope is replaced by a diverging lens. The length of the telescope is then adjusted until it becomes a working telescope again.
